headline: Your ears convert air vibrations into electrical signals your brain interprets as sound
universal_truth: We perceive only a narrow slice of what's happening around us
fun_facts: The three smallest bones in your body are in your ear—together they'd fit on a penny
Your ears also control balance—your inner ear detects head position and movement
Humans hear frequencies from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; dogs hear up to 65,000 Hz
discussion_questions: What sounds would you hear if your range extended beyond human limits?
How does knowing you only hear a narrow frequency band change your sense of reality?
Why do you think hearing and balance share the same organ?

hook.script: Right now, invisible waves are traveling through the air, entering your ear, bouncing off the tiniest bones in your body, and becoming electrical signals your brain interprets as sound. Hearing is vibration transformed—air movement becoming meaning.

cliff.script: Sound is just air pressure waves. Yet from these waves, you distinguish music from noise, recognize voices, locate sources, and perceive meaning. How does your ear convert simple vibrations into rich auditory experience?
cliff.prompt: How does the ear convert sound waves to signals?

options.text: Sound vibrates the eardrum, amplifies through tiny bones, and triggers hair cells that send electrical signals
options.response: Yes. Mechanical vibration is converted to electrical signals by delicate hair cells in the cochlea.

options.text: The ear canal focuses sound waves directly onto nerve endings
options.response: The canal helps, but the conversion process is more complex...

fact1.title: Tiny Bones
fact1.script: The three smallest bones in your body—hammer, anvil, and stirrup—are in your middle ear. Together, they amplify sound vibrations 20x before passing them to the inner ear. These bones fit on a penny and enable all hearing.

fact2.title: Hair Cell Magic
fact2.script: In your cochlea, 16,000 hair cells detect vibrations and convert them to electrical signals. Different areas respond to different frequencies. Unlike most cells, damaged hair cells don't regenerate—that's why hearing loss is often permanent.

fact3.title: Balance Bonus
fact3.script: Your inner ear also contains the vestibular system—fluid-filled chambers that detect head position and movement. That's why ear infections can cause dizziness. Hearing and balance share the same real estate.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: We perceive only a narrow slice of reality. Hearing reminds us that there's always more happening than we can detect. Dogs hear what we can't. Bats hear in echoes. Humility about our limits opens us to wonder.

outro.script: That's Day 85. Tomorrow, we'll explore why your heart never stops. Until then, listen closely—and appreciate the invisible vibrations your ears translate into meaning.

growTrack.title: Sound Attention - Listen Deeper
growTrack.activity: Close your eyes for 60 seconds and count how many distinct sounds you can hear—near, far, constant, intermittent. We usually filter out most sounds. How many were you missing before you paid attention?
